actions.justification: Mandatory action: Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, making hydration status critical before contrast administration. Dehydration significantly increases risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.
Mandatory action: Baseline eGFR is essential to quantify renal function in this CKD stage 4 patient prior to contrast exposure during cardiac catheterization.
Mandatory action: CKD stage 4 and diabetes are major risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. A comprehensive risk factor review guides pre-procedural prophylactic strategies.
Establish baseline vital signs prior to contrast administration; patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN).
Identify nephrotoxic medications (e.g., NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, metformin) that may need to be held before contrast administration in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient.
Calculate the maximum safe contrast volume based on eGFR to minimize CIN risk in this CKD stage 4 patient undergoing cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both high-risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN). Nephrology consultation is warranted prior to cardiac catheterization to optimize renal protection strategy.
Given CKD stage 4 and diabetes, consider whether contrast-free or lower-contrast imaging alternatives exist to reduce nephrotoxic contrast exposure before proceeding with catheterization.
CKD stage 4 with diabetes places this patient at high risk for AKI. Ensuring no additional nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.) are administered is a critical pre-procedural step.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure risk. Documenting the eGFR check establishes baseline renal function for contrast-induced nephropathy risk stratification and post-procedure monitoring.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.) prior to contrast exposure is a key preventive measure per CI-AKI guidelines.

Baseline urine output assessment is essential in a CKD stage 4 diabetic patient prior to contrast administration to guide hydration strategy and detect pre-existing oliguria that would increase CI-AKI risk.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes; metformin should be held before contrast administration to reduce risk of lactic acidosis, per standard pre-contrast guidelines.

IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid (e.g., normal saline or sodium bicarbonate) before cardiac catheterization is a cornerstone of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prevention in high-risk patients with CKD and diabetes.
CKD stage 4 significantly reduces drug clearance; medications used peri-procedurally (anticoagulants, sedatives, analgesics) should have doses adjusted to account for reduced renal function.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Holding nephrotoxic medications pre-procedure reduces additional renal insult risk.
Pre-procedure IV hydration and post-contrast hydration are key preventive strategies for contrast-induced nephropathy in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 and diabetes.

Patient with CKD stage 4 (likely eGFR consistent with G3b or lower) should have metformin held peri-procedure due to risk of lactic acidosis when combined with contrast exposure and potential acute kidney injury.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedure IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a key evidence-based intervention to reduce renal injury risk prior to cardiac catheterization.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD/diabetes patient undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of acute kidney injury and ensure adequate hydration response.
Serial serum creatinine measurement at 48-72 hours post-contrast is the standard of care to detect contrast-induced nephropathy in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 and diabetes.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Checking serum creatinine at 48 hours post-contrast is a standard monitoring step to detect AKI early.
Serial creatinine monitoring at 72 hours is recommended in high-risk patients (CKD + diabetes) post-contrast administration to capture delayed nephrotoxic injury.

Ensuring optimal fluid status prior to and during the procedure is essential in CKD stage 4 patients to minimize contrast-induced nephropathy risk. IV hydration strategy should be confirmed and maintained.
